summary_for_principal:
This closes the one loose end from the last round — a real gap I found but left alone at the time, since it wasn't what you'd asked for.

When one governed process calls another, the called one can end well, badly, or stop partway. Before this fix, if the author of the calling process forgot to capture that outcome, nothing downstream could ever know — a badly-ended call looked identical to a clean one. That's now refused, the same way this system already refuses other silently-dropped values.

This was closeable now because the field in question is always named the same, fixed thing internally. An earlier pass had judged the fuller version of this problem too ambiguous and correctly left it alone — guessing at an author's own naming would have been worse than the gap.

Three existing tests needed a one-line addition each to keep passing.

Full test suite: 414 passed, 2 new.

decisions.problem: A process call whose child ends badly (FAILED, STOPPED, or an engine-synthesised ending like FORBIDDEN) can be reported as the calling step's own plain SUCCESS when the calling Tool has no controls (or controls that pass regardless), because control-checking runs against the Tool's own mapped output dict — and if that dict's 'ending' key was never captured into state by the calling step's out: mapping, nothing downstream can ever read it, whatever it says.

decisions.cost_to_change: Low — both the validator rule and the engine refusal are simple additive checks; a future pass building the fuller requirement subsumes this one without needing to undo it.
